newsitem.title: USA: Barshefsky woos farmers for trade bill support.
newsitem.headline: Barshefsky woos farmers for trade bill support.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky heads to the heartland this week to hear farmers' complaints about U.S. trade with Canada and what they say is an unfair trade agreement.

Her appearance Wednesday at a public forum in Minot, N.D., is part of an overall effort by the newly confirmed U.S. Trade Representative to address a growing perception in the farm community that the North American Free Trade Agreement and some of the other big trade deals entered into in recent years may not be working as well as their signatories hoped.

"There is a feeling that the agreements have not been enforced as quickly as we would like to see," said one farm industry lobbyist. "There is a perception among farmers that NAFTA is not working for them."

The administration is taking notice. Farm industry support is essential if the White House hopes to get Congress, particularly the Senate, to pass new so-called fast track trade negotiation authority. The legislation is needed to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile and other trade deals without fear that lawmakers will change them.
President Clinton is sending Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman to Chile in May to try to work out some thorny agriculture trade issues.

Earlier this month the USTR launched an investigation into European Union modified starch subsidies at the request of the U.S. Wheat Gluten Industry Council, and Barshefsky is creating a new ambassador position soley devoted to farm trade issues.
Peter Scher, who was Mickey Kantor's chief of staff at the U.S. Trade Representative's Office and at the Commerce Department, is expected to be named to the post, sources said.

The administration had been expected to move quickly on fast track legislation this year, but so far no proposal has been presented to Congress. A USTR spokesman said the administration is still consulting with lawmakers and is likely to unveil a proposal by the end of April. Fast track was put on hold during the 1996 presidential campaign after Congress and the White House failed to agree on authority to negotiate labour and environmental issues.

Meanwhile, administration officials are laying the groundwork, and addressing farm country concerns about trade is a part of that effort, officials said. Barshefsky, who had been "acting" U.S. trade representative for nearly a year, may be looking forward to her first trip since being confirmed with some sense of dread.

Farmers are expected to vent their anger at what they fear will become a flood of Canadian wheat and barley into their markets as a result of some regulatory changes in Ottawa that suddenly have made U.S. markets more attractive to Canadian growers.
It is unfriendly territory for Barshefsky, who faces a tough battle in Congress to win the fast track authority.

Senator Byron Dorgan, who along with the two other members of the North Dakota U.S. congressional delegation is sponsoring the forum, plans to reintroduce legislation this year that could set the stage for a U.S. withdrawal from NAFTA unless certain conditions are met.

A ruling last year by a NAFTA dispute resolution panel upholding tariff decisions by Ottawa that effectively shut out U.S. poultry and dairy products from the Canadian market shocked U.S. farmers. Trade groups in Washington warned the White House earlier this year that they did not think they could muster enough support within the farm community for fast track trade negotiation authority.

The poultry and dairy decision "sent a very bad signal to the countryside, especially when the decision is five-to-zero and half of these guys are supposed to be on your own team," said an industry lobbyist.

Barshefsky is likely to argue that the trade negotiation authority is needed to continue work to open markets for U.S. agriculture, a top export industry that in the past supported both NAFTA and the global trade deal that created the World Trade Organisation.
"I don't think we have really had a chance to tell our story yet," said a USTR official.
